KNOWLEDGE BASE

“How Codex Happened” https://every.?ev_audience=free by Dan Shipper https://every.?ev_audience=free: A year ago, OpenAI’s coding effort looked lost: Codex Cloud had flopped, the Windsurf deal had fallen apart, and Claude Code was taking off. Then a tiny team in the “backwaters” of the company built an app that swallowed ChatGPT from the inside. Today, Codex and ChatGPT for Work together have 40 million weekly users. Dan Shipper https://every.?ev_audience=free spent months talking with the OpenAI team that made Codex happen, including Greg Brockman and Thibault Sottiaux, to learn what it takes to build when the frontier keeps moving. His story comes with prompts for applying the lessons to your own work, plus the full interview transcripts for paid subscribers.

Every software engineer Lee Knowlton turned Dan’s piece into an interactive visual novel. Watch a trailer for it, and play it here https://every.?ev_audience=free.

https://every.?ev_audience=free

Lee used Codex to generate cel-shaded anime avatars of Dan and his interview subjects and Claude to compose the experience and cut a trailer.

“Gemini 4 Argon Puts Google Back On the Frontier” https://every.?ev_audience=free by Katie Parrott https://every.?ev_audience=free/Vibe Check https://every.?ev_audience=free: Gemini 4 Argon brings Google back into the frontier pack, an impressive feat for a company that runs on Google Workspace. The model is strongest as a collaborator: Dan now switches to it to structure essays and sharpen metaphors, and Compound Engineering https://every.?ev_audience=free creator Kieran Klaassen https://every.?ev_audience=free found it a fast, capable prototyper even at its lowest effort setting. Left on its own, Argon overbuilds in prose and design, and its desktop app, Antigravity, feels six months to a year behind Claude Code and Codex.

🎧 🖥“The Best Founders Have Something AI Can’t Tell Them” https://every.?ev_audience=free by Laura Entis https://every.?ev_audience=free/Context Window https://every.?ev_audience=free: Matt Hartman, founder of Factorial Capital, talked to head of consulting Natalia Quintero https://every.?ev_audience=free on The Every Podcast https://every.?ev_audience=free about why he assumes every early-stage startup will pivot and backs technical founders who can build for whatever market comes next. When vetting, he also looks for an “earned insight”—a unique lesson only a founder could have learned—and the ability to keep finding new ones after launch. 🎧 🖥 Listen on Spotify https://every.?ev_audience=free or Apple Podcasts https://every._?ev_audience=free, watch on X https://every.?ev_audience=free or YouTube https://every.?ev_audience=free, or read the transcript https://every.?ev_audience=free. Also inside: a field report https://every.?ev_audience=free on FeanixBio, an agricultural technology startup that runs on agents in Slack, and head of social media Becky Isjwara https://every.?ev_audience=free on using the Every Agent as her onboarding buddy, with the prompts https://every.?ev_audience=free she recommends new hires try on day one.

“Context Engineering Is Knowing When to Start Over” https://every.?ev_audience=free by Mike Taylor https://every.?ev_audience=free/Also True for Humans https://every.?ev_audience=free: Mike keeps memory off in Claude and ChatGPT and starts a fresh thread for every task, even on the same project five minutes later. Context piles up inside a thread, he argues, and the model keeps following instructions you’ve moved on from and building on its own mistakes. He lays out seven ways that context goes wrong—including distraction, confusion, neglect, and poisoning—and pairs each with a sign to watch for and a fix, such as editing your earlier message instead of arguing with the AI.
